Title: RNAF: Regularization neural attenuation fields for sparse-view CBCT reconstruction
Text:
RNAF: Regularization neural attenuation
ﬁelds for sparse-view CBCT
reconstruction
Chunjie Xia1, Tianyun Gu2, Nan Zheng2,3, Hongjiang Wei2 and Tsung-Yuan Tsai2,3
Abstract
Cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) is increasingly used in clinical settings, with the radiation dose incurred during
X-ray acquisition emerging as a critical concern. Traditional algorithms for reconstructing high-quality CBCT images typ-
ically necessitate hundreds of X-ray projections, prompting a shift towards sparse-view CBCT reconstruction as a means
to minimize radiation exposure. A novel approach, leveraging the Neural Attenuation Field (NAF) based on neural radi-
ation ﬁeld algorithms, has recently gained traction. This method offers rapid and promising CBCT reconstruction out-
comes using a mere 50 views. Nonetheless, NAF tends to overlook the inherent structural properties of projected
images, which can lead to shortcomings in accurately capturing the structural essence of the object being imaged. To
address these limitations, we introduce an enhanced method: Regularization Neural Attenuation Fields (RNAF). Our
approach includes two key innovations. First, we implement a hash coding regularization technique designed to retain
low-frequency details within the reconstructed images, thereby preserving essential structural information. Second,
we incorporate a Local Patch Global (LPG) sampling strategy. This method focuses on extracting local geometric details
from the projection image, ensuring that the intensity variations in randomly sampled X-rays closely mimic those in the
actual projection image. Comparative analyses across various body parts (Chest, Jaw, Foot, Abdomen, Knee) reveal that
RNAF substantially outperforms existing algorithms. Speciﬁcally, its reconstruction quality exceeds that of previous
NeRF-based, optimization-based, and analysis algorithms by margins of at least 2.09 dB, 3.09 dB, and 13.84 dB respect-
ively. This signiﬁcant enhancement in performance underscores the potential of RNAF as a groundbreaking solution in
the realm of CBCT imaging, offering a path towards achieving high-quality reconstructions with reduced radiation expos-
ure. Our implementation is publically available at https://github.com/springXIACJ/FRNAF
Keywords
sparse-view CBCT reconstruction, regularization neural attenuation ﬁeld, local patch global

Introduction
Cone Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT) represents a
signiﬁcant advancement in medical imaging technology,
utilizing diverging kilovolt (kV) X-rays to produce detailed
visualizations of anatomical structures. Unlike traditional
Fan Beam CT (FBCT), CBCT excels in delivering superior
three-dimensional (3D) image quality while requiring sig-
niﬁcantly less time to conduct a scan. In a typical CBCT
procedure, the X-ray source moves uniformly along an arc-
shaped trajectory around the subject, emitting a cone-
shaped beam of X-rays at each position towards the target
organ. Positioned on the opposite side, the detector captures
these emissions as two-dimensional (2D) perspective pro-
jections.1 The goal of CBCT reconstruction is to assemble
these 2D projections into a coherent 3D attenuation map
of the targeted organ. This process is predominantly
achieved through the Filtered Back Projection (FBP) algo-
rithm.2 However, this technique necessitates capturing a

large number of views to maintain high image quality,
leading to concerns over the amount of X-ray radiation to
which patients are exposed. Recent research has focused
on reducing the radiation dose in CBCT exams, exploring
strategies
such
as
lowering
the
milliampere-seconds
(low-mAs) or decreasing the number of required projection
views (sparse-view).3 This paper delves into the speciﬁcs of
sparse-view CBCT reconstruction, highlighting its potential
to maintain imaging quality while minimizing radiation
exposure.
Sparse-view CBCT reconstruction is focused on accur-
ately determining 3D attenuation coefﬁcients from a
minimal set of 2D projections. This task is particularly chal-
lenging due to the limited amount of data available. To
improve the quality of reconstructions derived from
sparse projection data, various traditional methodologies
have been employed. These techniques leverage the con-
sistency between the acquired projections and the recon-
structed image. Broadly, these methods fall into three
main categories: analytical, iterative, and learning-based
techniques. Analytical methods aim to calculate the attenu-
ation coefﬁcients by directly solving the Radon transform
and its inverse.4 A prime example of this approach is the
Feldkamp-Davis-Kress
(FDK)2
algorithm,
which
is
widely utilized in CBCT reconstruction. On the other
hand, iterative methods approach reconstruction as a
process of minimization, continuously reﬁning the estimate
of the 3D attenuation coefﬁcients to reduce the discrepancy
between the actual 2D projections and their estimated
counterparts. An example of this strategy is seen in
the Simultaneous Algebraic Reconstruction Technique
(SART),5 which iteratively updates the 3D attenuation coef-
ﬁcients to minimize differences. Each of these approaches
offers distinct advantages and challenges in the quest to
achieve high-quality reconstructions from limited projec-
tion data, highlighting the ongoing innovation in CBCT
reconstruction techniques.
With the emergence of deep learning technologies,
methods for CBCT reconstruction that rely on learning
algorithms have become increasingly popular. These tech-
niques are primarily based on an encoder-decoder architec-
ture. Within this framework, a 2D encoder processes the
input projections to extract features. These features are
then transformed into a 3D format through a dimensional
reshaping process. Finally, a 3D decoder utilizes these
reshaped
features
to
create
a
detailed
volumetric
image.6,7,8,9 A novel category of methodologies, referred
to as Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF),10 has recently made
its mark by offering an innovative solution for creating
new viewpoints while concurrently estimating 3D volumet-
ric representations of scenes. NeRF conceptualizes the
underlying data as a continuous function that assigns
spatial coordinates to attributes like occupancy and color.
Despite their breakthroughs, existing NeRF models face
limitations in
their
expressive
capability.
A
notable
challenge is their inherent spectral biases,11 which restrict
the
representation
to
only
pre-speciﬁed
frequencies.
Consequently, there’s a growing consensus on the need to
incorporate additional frequency bases into neural net-
works,12,13 albeit at the expense of signiﬁcantly slower
convergence rates. In light of these challenges, hash value-
based methods have gained popularity.14 These methods
eschew traditional frequency encoding in favor of learnable
hash keys, which index data, thereby mitigating the effects
of spectral biases.15
Present methods for CBCT reconstruction utilizing
NeRF generally adopt a basic approach for ray sampling
at the pixel level during the training stage.15,16 This
involves randomly selecting X-rays that correlate with scat-
tered pixels throughout the entire projection image. This
approach leads to a suboptimal extraction of the geometric
structural information embedded within the projection
image. Moreover, given the sparse distribution of X-ray
projections in space, the random sampling technique may
yield a low efﬁciency in sampling, often capturing areas
that fall into the background, thus not contributing valuable
data for reconstruction.
To tackle existing challenges, we introduce an innova-
tive framework termed Regularization Neural Attenuation
Fields (RNAF). This framework adopts a self-supervised
methodology to reconstruct 3D CBCT images from X-ray
projections without relying on external CBCT scans. At
the core of RNAF is a multilayer perceptron (MLP) that
processes encoded spatial coordinates and outputs attenu-
ation coefﬁcients for those coordinates. Unlike traditional
approaches, recent studies have utilized sinusoidal func-
tions at different frequencies to enhance input mapping
to higher-dimensional spaces. However, this method
tends to overﬁt when the data is scarce, as seen in the
standard NeRF encoding with sinusoidal functions.10 To
address this, FreeNeRF17 presents a novel concept of
sinusoidal frequency regularization, adjusting the fre-
quency bands of NeRF’s inputs to ensure a stable learning
curve and prevent early training overﬁtting. RNAF draws
inspiration from FreeNeRF,17 applying regularization in
the hash encoding phase to preserve low-frequency
details in the reconstruction, thereby enhancing image
quality.
Additionally, RNAF innovates with a local patch ray
sampling technique that leverages thresholds to identify
and isolate foreground regions rich in critical projection
image information. It then crops non-overlapping patches
from these regions for X-ray sampling on patch pixels,
helping the MLP better understand local 2D structures.
For areas outside these patches, it employs random X-ray
sampling based on the NAF protocol.15 Remarkably,
RNAF
operates
solely
on
available
projection
data
without needing external datasets or structural priors,
setting a new standard in image reconstruction quality.
Our experimental ﬁndings robustly indicate that RNAF

Related works
Sparse-View CBCT reconstruction
Traditional cone beam CT reconstruction techniques can be
classiﬁed into three main approaches: analytical, iterative,
and learning-based. Analytical methods, which involve
solving the Radon transform and its inverse, are capable
of producing high-quality reconstructions when provided
with hundreds of projections.4 However, their performance
diminishes
with
sparsely
sampled
projection
data,
often resulting in noticeable striping artifacts in CBCT
images.2 On the other hand, iterative methods approach
reconstruction as a process of minimization, incorporating
an optimization framework alongside a regularization
module.5,18,19 Although these methods are adept at man-
aging noise and data insufﬁciency, they can sometimes
degrade the overall image quality.18 In recent years, convo-
lutional
neural
networks
(CNNs)6,7,8
and
diffusion
models20 have been explored for sparse-view CBCT recon-
struction, offering promising results. One of the prominent
models is the Iterative Residual Optimization Network for
Limited-Angle
Tomographic
Reconstruction.21
This
model leverages iterative optimization techniques to reﬁne
reconstruction
results
progressively.
By
focusing
on
residual learning, it effectively reduces artifacts and
improves the ﬁdelity of reconstructed images, particularly
in scenarios where data is limited due to angular constraints.
Another signiﬁcant contribution is the Wavelet-Improved
Score-Based Generative Model for Medical Imaging.22
This model integrates wavelet transformations with score-
based generative modeling to enhance the reconstruction
of medical images. The wavelet transformation aids in cap-
turing multi-scale features, while the generative model pro-
vides a robust framework for reconstructing high-quality
images
from
sparse
data
inputs.
The
Multi-channel
Optimization
Generative
Model
for
Stable
Ultra-
Sparse-View CT Reconstruction represents a breakthrough
in handling ultra-sparse data scenarios.23 By optimizing
across multiple channels, this model stabilizes the recon-
struction process, ensuring that the output remains consist-
ent and reliable even when the input data is extremely
limited. This approach is particularly beneﬁcial for CT
applications where reducing radiation exposure is critical.
Lastly, Dual-Domain Collaborative Diffusion Sampling
introduces a novel approach for the reconstruction of
Multi-Source Stationary Computed Tomography. The
DCDS model addresses the issues of artifacts and inaccur-
ate projections in the reconstruction process by integrating
the diffusion processes in both the sinogram and image
domains.
By
leveraging
information
from
multiple
sources, this model achieves superior results in stationary
computed tomography, surpassing the capabilities of trad-
itional methods.24 These advanced diffusion models col-
lectively represent a signiﬁcant leap forward in the ﬁeld
of limited-data tomographic reconstruction. They not only
address the challenges posed by sparse data but also set
the stage for future innovations in medical imaging and
beyond. Through their unique methodologies and applica-
tions, these models contribute to the ongoing evolution of
tomographic reconstruction techniques. Despite their poten-
tial, these learning-based methods require extensive data-
sets for network training and sometimes fail to capture
essential ﬁne details,24,25 resulting in overly smooth
images. Additionally, their dependence on neural networks
to “remember” CBCT appearances poses challenges in
transferring a trained model from one application to
another due to the speciﬁcity of the learned features. To
overcome these challenges, we have developed a novel
algorithm based on NeRF. This approach aims to address
the limitations of current reconstruction techniques by
leveraging the strengths of both iterative and learning-based
methods, providing a more versatile and robust solution for
CBCT reconstruction.
Neural radiance ﬁelds
NeRF10 leverages neural networks to transform 3D spatial
coordinates into values like color and density, utilizing a
collection of 2D views. In this framework, positional encod-
ing plays a critical role. It transforms low-dimensional input
features into high-dimensional ones, enhancing the net-
work’s ability to capture both high and low-frequency com-
ponents in the input image, rather than skewing towards the
latter.12,13 Despite NeRF’s notable achievements, its ori-
ginal iteration had drawbacks, such as the need for numer-
ous input views and extensive optimization periods. To
address these issues, hash tables were introduced.14 They
effectively manage the memory allocated to trainable fea-
tures, facilitating the creation of compact yet detailed fea-
tures and expediting the optimization process. The use of
a hash encoder-based approach, initially applied to sparse
Xia et al.
715


view CBCT reconstruction by NAF,15 is particularly note-
worthy. This method capitalizes on 3D geometry awareness
and the consistency across multiple views inherent in neural
rendering. Moreover, it incorporates multi-resolution hash
encoding, achieving remarkable detail preservation even
with a limited set of 50 projections. However, it’s important
to recognize that NAF’s reliance on a small number of
images makes it more vulnerable to noise. This sensitivity
can amplify high-frequency components, which, in turn,
may obstruct the network’s ability to delve into low-
frequency information. Such a limitation can impede the
learning of coherent geometric structures, posing a signiﬁ-
cant challenge to the model’s effectiveness.26
Method
CBCT scanning
As depicted in Figure 1, in the process of CBCT scanning,
the X-ray source revolves around the object along a planar
arc trajectory, emitting a cone-shaped X-ray beam to
capture 2D projection images of speciﬁc human organs
such as lungs and knees. Speciﬁcally, the X-ray source
moves in ﬁxed angular increments from the initial point
to the ﬁnal point of the predetermined arc trajectory,
while the 2D panel records the X-ray projections at
uniform angular intervals. For instance, it progresses
within the angular range [0180) with an angular step of
3.6 degrees, resulting in the acquisition of 50 2D projected
images. It is important to note that, in the context of this
paper, the data collection angle spans from 0 to 180 degrees.
Neural radiance ﬁelds
Figure 2 illustrates an overview of our RNAF framework. In
the context of sparse-view CBCT reconstruction, we
employ a NeRF with a MLP to represent a scene as a volu-
metric density ﬁeld μ for each point within the scene.10 In
RNAF, it takes a 3D coordinate x ∈R3 as input and pro-
duces the corresponding density as output. As its core,
RNAF learns a continuous function fθ(x) = μ, where θ
denotes MLP parameters.

through the internal medium of the cube. To accurately
reconstruct the internal structure, we sample N points at
intersections where the X-ray paths cross within the cube.
This approach differs fundamentally from NeRF’s tech-
nique, which uses volume rendering to simulate surface
properties. Our method, essential for CBCT reconstruction,
focuses on authentic volume rendering. Our goal is to
ensure comprehensive coverage of the cube’s entire
volume by utilizing all the sampled points along every
X-ray path. This requires us to distribute the sampling
points as evenly as possible along each path. To achieve
this, we begin by identifying the near and far points of
each ray, determined by the reconstruction volume’s dimen-
sions. We then apply a hierarchical sampling strategy,10
dividing the path between these points into N equally
spaced intervals. Within each interval, we uniformly
select a point, ensuring a thorough and uniform sampling
across the volume. By choosing N to exceed the required
CT image resolution, we guarantee that every grid cell
penetrated by an X-ray is represented by at least one
sample. The coordinates of these sampling points are then
processed by the position encoding module, enabling
precise volume reconstruction.

MLPs can serve as universal function approximators,
recent research has uncovered a phenomenon known as
“spectral bias”. This bias implies that neural networks,
including MLPs, tend to excel in learning low-frequency
ﬁne-grained
details.11,27

Volume rendering. In our approach for CBCT reconstruction,
we utilize a conventional MLP Φ to represent the bounded
ﬁeld. This MLP takes spatial coordinates encoded with reg-
ularized hash encoder feature vectors as input and yields the
attenuation coefﬁcient μ at that particular spatial location, as
illustrated in Figure 2 c. The architecture of our MLP is
meticulously crafted, comprising 4 fully connected layers,
each endowed with the Rectiﬁed Linear Unit (ReLU) activa-
tion function and equipped with 32 channels. To enhance the
network’s efﬁciency and accuracy, we’ve incorporated a
skip connection strategy. This allows the input of the
network to be concatenated directly to the activation of the
second layer, fostering a more robust and error-resilient
model. Following the ﬁnal layer’s output, we apply a
Softplus activation function to generate the volume density.

intensity gradually diminishes. Ultimately, the attenuated
X-rays are captured by a ﬂat-panel detector, producing
pixel-level intensity values. This process is typically
described by the Beer-Lambert Law28 and is simulated
using numerical methods to model the attenuation process:

In this paper, we generate the projected image Ipred from the
attenuation ﬁeld using Eq.4 and subsequently learn the
neural attenuation ﬁeld by minimizing the L2 loss
between the generated projection and the actual projection.
The loss function is deﬁned as follows:

Ultimately, we construct a voxel grid of the desired size.
Based on the required voxel size and spatial resolution for
the actual CBCT, we calculate the spatial coordinates corre-
sponding to each voxel. These voxel spatial coordinates are
then fed into a position encoder and a trained MLP to
predict the attenuation coefﬁcient at each corresponding
position, facilitating the reconstruction of CBCT.
As shown in Figure 3 (a), existing CBCT reconstruction
based on NeRF primarily employ a simplistic pixel-level
ray sampling strategy during the training phase.15,16 They
randomly sample scattered pixels across the entire projected
image. This sampling method does not capture the semantic
information of adjacent pixels, so its ability to measure the
similarity between the projection image and the X-ray
image is limited. Secondly, during the random sampling
process, there may be some X-rays falling on the back-
ground area of the projected image. These X-rays do not
penetrate the object and cannot characterize the radiation
density characteristics of the object, thus reducing the learn-
ing efﬁciency of the model.
To address these problems, we proposed a Local Patch
and Global (LPG) ray sampling strategy, as shown in
Figure 3 (b). We ﬁrst use a threshold T=0 to segment the fore-
ground part of the projection image. Subsequently, to avoid
redundant sampling, we divide the projected image I into a
set W ∈RHW/S2×S×S of HW / S2 non-overlapping windows
with size S × S. Let Wf denote the set of windows that are
entirely contained in the foreground regions as
Wf = {w ∈W}
To capture the local semantic information of objects, we
perform patch-level sampling. Speciﬁcally, we randomly
select the Nl window Wl = {w1, ... , wNl} from Wf , as
shown by the red patch in Figure 3 (b). In addition, to help
the model better capture global information, we perform pixel-
level sampling. In particular, we randomly select Ng pixels
from the foreground regions, excluding the Wl area, to avoid
repeated ray sampling, as shown by the blue pixels in
Figure 3(b). Using the LPG ray sampling strategy, the model
can capture information more efﬁciently and model the geom-
etry of the imaged object on a two-dimensional projection.
Experiments
Simulation settings
Dataset. We conduct experiments on ﬁve datasets con-
taining human organ. Details are listed in Table 1. As
with the data in NAF, we evaluate our method using
public datasets of human organ CT, including chest,
jaw, foot, and abdomen. The chest data is from the
LIDC-IDRI dataset29 and the rest of the data is from

the Open Science Visualization Dataset.30 we also
employ a knee CT dataset to validate the merits of our
proposed approach.
Given the scarcity of clinically paired 2D projection data and
3D CBCT images and the prevalence of volumetric CT scans,
we address this challenge by generating multiple X-ray projec-
tions from volumetric CT images using digital reconstruction
radiography(DRR)technology,implementedthroughtheopen-
source tomography toolbox known as TIGRE.31 Then we use
the TIGRE to generate projections by scanning CT volumes
with 3% noise in the range of 0◦∼180◦.
We employ this set of projection data to train our model
independently, Subsequently, we utilize the trained model
to generate reconstructed CBCT body data based on
voxel position information. During training, ground truth
data is generated by producing multiple X-ray projections
from volumetric CT images using the DRR technique.
The performance of the model is evaluated by comparing
the results with the original volumetric CT data.
Furthermore, we positioned the head phantom on a rotat-
ing platform to acquire projection data using dynamic
digital radiography technology. The turntable executed a
complete 360-degree rotation, resulting in a total of 360
projection views with dimensions of 1536 × 1536 pixels.
We employed the FDK algorithm to reconstruct a 512 ×
512 × 512 CT image from the full set of projection data,
serving as the ground truth. For our experiments, only 50
projections were utilized to assess the effectiveness of our
method on real-world equipment.
Implementation details. Our proposed method is implemen-
ted based on the Pytorch framework.32 We utilize the Adam
optimizer33 (β1 = 0.9 and β2 = 0.999) for 3000 iterations
with an initial learning rate of 1e-3, which exponentially
decays to 1e-5 during the optimization process. The batch-
size |B| of X-rays in set to 2048, 1024 of which is from the
local-patch-level sampling and the local-patch size is 4 × 4
and the other 1024 is from the global pixel-level sampling.
We uniformly sample 320 points along each X-ray. For
each scene, we use its 50 projections to train, another 50
projections to test the performance of its CT volume to
evaluate the results of CT reconstruction. All experiments
are conducted on an RTX 4090 GPU.
Comparison methods and evaluation metrics. Our proposed
method is compared against ﬁve baseline techniques, i.e.,
FDK,2 SART,5 ASD-POCS,18 InTomo,16 FreeNerf,17 and
NAF.15 In our experiment, we employ two commonly used
indicators to evaluate the sparse-view CBCT reconstruction
performance, i.e., Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) and
Structural Similarity (SSIM).34 PSNR assessed artifact sup-
pression performance, while SSIM measured the perceptual
difference between two signals. Higher PNSR/SSIM values
correspond to more accurate reconstruction results.
CBCT reconstruction results
Quantitative and qualitative results. A quantitative compari-
son of the reconstruction results produced by various
methods are presented in Table 2. For the sake of fairness,
we do not compare algorithms based on learning from a
large number of projection-CT pairs, but focus on compar-
ing methods that only require X-ray projections for training
or direct processing. Our method signiﬁcantly outperforms
all other methods in terms of PSNR and SSIM. Notably, in
50 projection views, the performance of RNAF is at least
2.09, 3.09, and 13.84 dB higher than the previous algorithm
NeRF-based, optimization-based and analysis.
Qualitatively, we provide visualization of the results

Applications
Our objective with RNAF is to attain high-quality CBCT
reconstruction utilizing sparse-view data. To substantiate
the practical utility of our reconstruction algorithm in clin-
ical settings, we conducted a direct knee joint bone tissue
segmentation on the reconstructed knee joint CBCT
images, as illustrated in Figure 8. The precision of the 3D
knee joint model’s surface shape was independently evalu-
ated by aligning the 3D models generated from segmenta-
tion of the RNAF reconstruction with the 3D reference
model derived from the original CT scans. A 3D/3D
surface rough registration was accomplished by employing
the principal inertia axes computed from the vertex sets of
both models, Subsequently, an iterative closest point
(ICP)36 rigid alignment was applied to minimize the inter-
surface distance.37 Based on the segmentation of the knee
joint’s skeletal structure, the distance error at the distal
end of the femur was 0.16 ± 0.29 mm, at the proximal end
of the tibia, was 0.15 ± 0.30 mm, and at the patella, it was
0.20 ± 0.42 mm, as shown in Figure 9.
Limitations and future work
While RNAF can provide high-frequency CBCT reconstruc-
tion results with as few as 10 views, it may encounter chal-
lenges when dealing with limited input data, such as only 5
views. CBCT reconstruction relies on a ﬁxed number of
voxels and spatial resolution. Therefore, future improvements
can be made by optimizing the neural attenuation ﬁeld based
on ﬁxed spatial positions, reducing the sampling points along
the rays, enhancing computational efﬁciency, and enabling
CBCT reconstruction on ultra-sparse views.

area in medical diagnostics that greatly beneﬁts from
precise, high-quality reconstructions. Our focus is on
addressing the challenge of capturing the complex struc-
tures that X-rays penetrate to reconstruct high-quality
CBCT images. To tackle this, we introduce a groundbreak-
ing framework named RNAF, speciﬁcally designed to sig-
niﬁcantly elevate the quality of CBCT reconstructions.
Understanding the importance of preserving intricate
details in medical imaging, our approach incorporates a
unique hash coding regularization technique. This innov-
ation ensures that low-frequency details, crucial for accurate
diagnostics, are maintained in the reconstructed images.
Furthermore, to capture the local geometric nuances and
the intensity variations that are inherent in actual projection
images, we have developed the Local Projection Geometry
(LPG) sampling strategy. This technique is pivotal in ensur-
ing that the intensity variation of randomly sampled X-rays
mirrors that of the actual projection images closely. Our
extensive testing across various body parts, including the
chest, jaw, feet, abdomen, and knee, demonstrates that
RNAF outperforms existing algorithms by a signiﬁcant
margin. These promising results underscore RNAF’s poten-
tial as a game-changing solution in the ﬁeld of CBCT
imaging. By offering a path to high-quality reconstructions,
RNAF not only aims to enhance diagnostic precision but
also contributes to reducing radiation exposure for patients.
This research marks a signiﬁcant step forward in our
quest to improve medical imaging technologies. It opens
new avenues for further exploration and development in
the ﬁeld, with the potential to bring about transformative
changes in how medical imaging is approached. We
invite fellow researchers, medical professionals, and tech-
nology enthusiasts to delve into our ﬁndings and explore
the possibilities that RNAF presents for the future of
CBCT imaging.

Abstract: Cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) is increasingly used in clinical settings, with the radiation dose incurred during X-ray acquisition emerging as a critical concern. Traditional algorithms for reconstructing high-quality CBCT images typ- ically necessitate hundreds of X-ray projections, prompting a shift towards sparse-view CBCT reconstruction as a means to minimize radiation exposure. A novel approach, leveraging the Neural Attenuation Field (NAF) based on neural radi- ation ﬁeld algorithms, has recently gained traction. This method offers rapid and promising CBCT reconstruction out- comes using a mere 50 views. Nonetheless, NAF tends to overlook the inherent structural properties of projected images, which can lead to shortcomings in accurately capturing the structural essence of the object being imaged. To address these limitations, we introduce an enhanced method: Regularization Neural Attenuation Fields (RNAF). Our approach includes two key innovations. First, we implement a hash coding regularization technique designed to retain low-frequency details within the reconstructed images, thereby preserving essential structural information. Second, we incorporate a Local Patch Global (LPG) sampling strategy. This method focuses on extracting local geometric details from the projection image, ensuring that the intensity variations in randomly sampled X-rays closely mimic those in the actual projection image. Comparative analyses across various body parts (Chest, Jaw, Foot, Abdomen, Knee) reveal that RNAF substantially outperforms existing algorithms. Speciﬁcally, its reconstruction quality exceeds that of previous NeRF-based, optimization-based, and analysis algorithms by margins of at least 2.09 dB, 3.09 dB, and 13.84 dB respect- ively. This signiﬁcant enhancement in performance underscores the potential of RNAF as a groundbreaking solution in the realm of CBCT imaging, offering a path towards achieving high-quality reconstructions with reduced radiation expos- ure. Our implementation is publically available at https://github.com/springXIACJ/FRNAF
